19  18. Governing Under Uncertainty

title: 18. Governing Under Uncertainty
text:
18.2 Horizon scanning
Horizon scanning is the operating discipline that keeps a governance program from being surprised by exactly the kind of change section 18.1 described. It needs a named owner and a defined set of actors, in addition to the structure this book has already given every other governance process. That structure has defined sources, a cadence, a triage step, and a translation of what is found into something the rest of the program can act on and eventually closes. A scanning owner collects; a qualified analyst assesses status and applicability; legal counsel owns the authoritative legal interpretation where one is needed rather than leaving that judgment to whoever read the source first. The affected system and business owners assess impact; an authorized decision-maker approves the resulting action; and, for a material change, assurance validates that closure actually happened instead of accepting a status update at face value.
Source selection means identifying a specific, finite set of places regulatory change will actually appear before it reaches general news coverage. Those places are the relevant regulator’s own rulemaking docket, legislative tracking services for jurisdictions where the organization operates, industry association bulletins, and, for frontier obligations specifically, the small number of standards bodies whose work determines when a conformity presumption becomes available at all. They also include the court docket for any litigation testing an obligation already in force. That is the source that would have surfaced Colorado’s stipulated stay directly, not the later docket that replaced the statute it stayed. Reading whatever a general news feed happens to surface is not horizon scanning; it is reacting to whatever a search algorithm decided was newsworthy, weeks after the docket entry that mattered was actually filed. Whatever a source captures, it needs to capture with the source’s own authoritative text, publisher, version, status, date, and a stable locator. A secondary summary of a rule is not the same kind of evidence as the rule itself. Section 18.3 develops why that precision matters once the source feeds a mapping card’s own trigger test.
Cadence is a risk decision, not a universal fixed interval. No single schedule catches every kind of change with enough lead time to matter. A court order, a final rule, a security directive, and a supplier’s own contract notice do not arrive on the same clock a legislative tracking service does. The right design sets a service level per source and per obligation, uses automated alerts where an authoritative source provides them, scheduled review for slower-moving sources, and event-driven escalation for court orders, final rules, incidents, and provider notices. This is different from checking every source on the same calendar regardless of how fast that particular source actually moves.
Triage is more than a two-way split between what to watch and what to act on immediately. A proposal’s own lead time can be shorter than the implementation time a response would need. A signed law, too, can turn out not to apply to the organization, the actor, the system, the territory, or the date at all. A workable triage scores each item on the authority of its source, its legal status, its applicability to what the organization actually does, and the probability it takes effect as drafted. It also scores the item’s lead time, its impact if it does take effect, its reversibility, what else depends on it, and the actual decision deadline. It then assigns the item to one of several states, not only two. Those states are watch, analyze, prepare, implement, challenge, pause, and close. A proposed bill with a short statutory lead time and a high probability of passage can legitimately land in prepare rather than watch. A signed law that plainly does not reach the organization’s own actors or systems can legitimately close without ever becoming an active change request.
Translation and the steps after it connect horizon scanning to everything else this book has built. A regulatory change that clears triage becomes a tracked change request carrying, at minimum, its owner, scope, source, legal status, applicability analysis, decision, implementation evidence, validation, and a closure date, in exactly the sense Chapter 15 already established for a requirement’s own record generally. That is different from a fact noted in an email and left to whoever happens to remember it when the next audit runs. A missed deadline, a conflicting authority, an unavailable source, a failed control, or uncertain scope escalates instead of stalling silently. Restriction, a pause, a rollback, seeking relief, or decommissioning are the actual responses available, depending on what the escalation finds. Closure records what the change revealed and updates the source list, the cadence, or the mapping structure when the case shows one of them missed something, rather than filing the outcome away unexamined. This same change record is what has to reach into the rest of the program, not terminate at the horizon-scanning desk. A change that alters a system’s applicable duties needs the same authority Chapter 17 gives to a target-model change. A change that originates in a supplier’s own notice, rather than a regulator’s, needs the vendor-relationship handling Chapter 16 already established for a supplier-initiated change. An organization building both need not unify them into a single schema; keeping the two record types separate, each cross-referencing the other, is a reasonable working choice. The Colorado sequence is a worked illustration of the complete lifecycle rather than only its translation step. A well-run horizon-scanning practice opens a change request at SB25B-004’s passage, with the bill text and its enactment date as the source, the organization’s Colorado-covered systems as the applicability, and a decision to prepare toward the amended date. It revises that request at the stipulated stay, recording that enforcement was suspended while the underlying obligation was not yet repealed, and deciding to pause implementation while keeping the assessment work already done. It then closes the original request and opens a new one at SB26-189’s enactment, recording that the prior statute was repealed and replaced and reanalyzing applicability against the new statute’s different duties. The decision is to rebuild the change record from the new statute’s actual text instead of carrying the old one forward. Each version is dated, retained, and tied to the same underlying system records. That way, a later question about what the organization believed it had to comply with, and when, has an answer traceable to a specific source and decision, rather than to memory.

title: 18. Governing Under Uncertainty
text:
18.3 Regulation-agnostic design
Chapter 3 established the mechanism this section extends. One shared fact record supports one mapping rule per applicable regulation, and each regulation’s own dated trigger is evaluated against those facts independently. No jurisdiction’s conclusion is fed into another’s rule as though it were itself a fact. What section 18.1 and section 18.2 add to that mechanism is the case it was built for. A regulation’s own trigger is not a fixed input; it is itself subject to deferral, amendment, or the kind of full repeal and reenactment Colorado’s sequence produced. Colorado’s statute, New York City’s Local Law 144, and every other regulation that might apply to the same system each define their own covered objects, actors, triggers, exclusions, and duties. Each can also change on its own schedule, without the others moving at all.







Figure 19.1: Figure 18.1. Regulation-agnostic mapping architecture



Read Figure 18.1 as three connected structures, not one. One of those structures is a fact record that never itself states a legal conclusion. Another is a set of independent mapping cards, one per applicable regulation, each running its own dated legal trigger against the same shared facts. The third is a change-handling structure that treats a legal change and a system-fact change as two separate kinds of event feeding the same downstream analysis, decision, and closure steps. A regulation changing, whether by deferral, amendment, or full repeal and reenactment as Colorado’s did, updates only that regulation’s own mapping card. The fact record does not change because the law changed. It describes what the system does and to whom, not what any particular law currently calls that. A system’s own facts changing, a new population, an added capability, a different deployment location, is the other entry into the same change-handling structure. Re-evaluating every regulation’s mapping card against the new facts, rather than assuming an old classification still holds, is what that second entry exists to force.
This is also where Chapter 2’s point about regulatory machinery connects forward. A mapping card’s trigger test has to encode a regulation’s actual statutory or annex text, not a paraphrase of it, which means someone has to have read the specific provision the card references. A card built from a paraphrase misfires the moment the regulation’s own text diverges from the shorthand an organization has been using internally. Maintaining each mapping card as a dated, versioned artifact, with its own legal-review and next-review fields, is what lets an organization answer, months or years later, exactly which obligations applied to a given system under a given regulation on a given date. That is a question section 18.2’s horizon-scanning record and this section’s mapping structure together are built to answer without reconstruction from memory.

19  18. Governing Under Uncertainty

title: 18. Governing Under Uncertainty
text:
18.4 What stays stable
Beneath the specific vocabulary of any given regulation, whether it calls a document a data protection impact assessment, an AI impact assessment, or nothing at all, a small set of reusable governance capabilities recurs across many of the frameworks this book has examined. These capabilities do not recur as identical legal duties, however. A specific regulation may require a given capability in full, require only a narrower piece of it, permit it without requiring it, or omit it entirely. This section names the capabilities themselves, instead of claiming that every regulation demands each one alike. Know what you have. An inventory, the subject of Chapter 3, is useful independently of which regulation asks for one, and several of the regulations this book has covered require it directly. Assess before deploying. An impact or risk assessment, Chapter 14’s subject, is required in some form by several frameworks and is good practice regardless of whether a specific statute names it. Test for disparate effect. Chapter 7’s fairness testing answers a question several consequential-decision frameworks ask in some form, whether the question is named algorithmic discrimination, disparate impact, or an equal-opportunity standard, though not every applicable regulation imposes a testing duty as such. Document. Chapter 15’s evidence discipline produces a record several regulations ask an organization to produce on demand, and some regulations require considerably less documentation than others. Oversee. A human review point, Chapter 8’s subject, appears under several frameworks governing automated decisions about people, though the scope of required oversight varies by regulation and by use case. Monitor. Chapter 9’s ongoing performance and drift monitoring answers whether a system still behaves the way its initial assessment assumed, a capability few regulations mandate in that specific form but that a well-run program benefits from regardless. Respond. Chapter 10’s incident process is what several regulations’ breach or serious-incident notification duties presuppose already exists, though notification triggers, deadlines, and recipients differ by regulation.
A program built on this convergent capability set is positioned to survive a regulation changing its name for a requirement, its exact threshold, or even its entire enforcement architecture. The inventory, the assessment, the testing, the documentation, the oversight point, the monitoring, and the incident process it built stay useful infrastructure regardless of which specific regulation’s vocabulary currently describes them. This is a claim about what the capabilities make available to an organization when a regulation changes, not a documented finding about how organizations that held Colorado’s replaced statute actually fared. What such a program loses when a regulation changes is the specific vocabulary and the specific threshold, both of which the mapping structure in section 18.3 is built to absorb. What it does not lose is the underlying capability the vocabulary was describing, provided the new regulation’s own trigger is checked against that capability, not assumed to match the old regulation’s.

19  18. Governing Under Uncertainty

title: 18. Governing Under Uncertainty
text:
18.5 The profession
What this field asks of the people who practice it is a specific, uncommon combination, not any one deep specialization. Technical literacy without technical expertise means enough grasp of how a model is built, tested, and deployed to ask a developer a real question and recognize an evasive answer, without needing to be able to build the model personally. Legal literacy without legal training means enough grasp of how an obligation is structured, and enough of the actual habit of reading a statute’s own text rather than a secondary summary of it, to spot an issue and gather the relevant facts. It also means being able to draft a candidate mapping rule for section 18.3’s structure, without that draft becoming authoritative on its own. That last qualification matters on its own terms. Issue-spotting and evidence assembly are not the same activity as authoritative legal interpretation. A mapping rule needs a named, qualified legal owner, a documented review before it governs a live system, and a clear escalation and appeal path for a disputed reading, not resting on whichever practitioner drafted it first. Judgment to distinguish real risk from theater, the distinction Chapter 17 named directly and this book has returned to throughout, applies now to an entire regulatory landscape rather than to one program. The practitioner has to be able to tell a genuine new obligation from a compliance vendor’s marketing about one. Standing to say no is the fourth quality, and the rarest of the four, the one no amount of technical or legal literacy substitutes for. It is not a personal trait some practitioners happen to have, but a delegated authority an organization has to grant on record, with its own scope, review, and escalation path, before the moment it is needed. That way, a business sponsor hears that a deployment does not proceed as designed from someone the organization has actually agreed in advance can say so, instead of discovering only in the moment that no one clearly can.
Where the discipline is heading remains unsettled on more than one axis. The United States Senate stripped a proposed decade-long moratorium on state AI enforcement from a 2025 reconciliation bill by a vote of 99 to 1. That is the clearest available evidence that the question of federal preemption is contested on grounds other than party. That means an organization operating across US states cannot assume the current patchwork of state law will simplify by federal action on any predictable timeline. Colorado’s own rulemaking on its replacement statute remained in progress when this chapter was checked on 13 September 2026, with the Attorney General’s public comment period open and a revised draft still pending. Even the specific state whose sequence this chapter uses as its central example has not finished settling its own rules. A reader arriving at this book after either of those developments has resolved should treat this chapter’s account of them as a demonstration of the horizon-scanning discipline section 18.2 describes, not as a claim that the landscape has stopped moving.
crumbs: Part V: Building Governance Capability
19  18. Governing Under Uncertainty

title: 18. Governing Under Uncertainty
text:
18.6 From compliance to advantage
This book’s own argument, made most directly in Chapter 4 and repeated here rather than newly established, is that a governance program’s cost is best justified by preventing a system that should never have been built from consuming a year of engineering time. That happens before someone finally asks whether the system should exist. Governance that instead spends its effort documenting the right system after the fact protects the organization’s evidentiary position without preventing the more expensive failure a wrong system produces in the first place. That is this book’s rationale for where governance’s value concentrates, not a demonstrated finding independent of the argument that produced it. Stating it plainly as a rationale is worth more than dressing it in the language of competitive differentiation that the evidence available to this book does not actually support. No rigorous, generalizable finding establishes that AI governance produces a market advantage distinguishable from ordinary risk avoidance. A reader who wants that specific claim should look elsewhere for it, not to this book, which has tried throughout to say only what its sources support.

title: 18. Governing Under Uncertainty
section: Case in focus: three systems, three years later
text:
Case in focus: three systems, three years later
MEDASSIST · FAIRLEND · TALENTSCREEN · Hypothetical, following the running cases
MedAssist’s community hospital gap, the delayed sepsis alerts Chapter 10 traced to three parallel contributing factors spanning testing, monitoring, and process, prompted the remediation this book has already described. Northfield’s subsequent effort to demonstrate compliance under Chapter 15’s evidence discipline then surfaced that the underlying acceptance criteria had never actually been written down. Northfield has since written them. Whether the community hospital population’s performance now genuinely matches the academic center’s, or merely produces a cleaner-looking record than before, is a question this book cannot answer from outside Northfield’s own ongoing monitoring. Neither can Northfield’s governance function answer it with full confidence yet, since a single remediation cycle is not the same as a demonstrated pattern across the population the original gap affected.
FairLend’s boundary dispute between AI governance and model risk management, the eighteen-month process Chapter 13 traced, resolved into the working division of authority that chapter described. The division has held for the deployments that have gone through it since. Whether it holds the next time a deployment falls on the boundary, rather than cleanly on one side of it, the way Chapter 13 itself acknowledged some future case eventually will, remains untested. Meridian has not yet had one.
TalentScreen’s governance program, Chapter 17’s sequencing failure and correction, now runs a properly tiered process across all three of Calloway’s systems in that composite case. What Calloway has not yet done is extend the same tiered discipline to whatever it adds to its portfolio next. Chapter 17’s own argument was that a target operating model earns nothing by existing on paper for a system count that has already grown past it. Calloway’s inventory, per Chapter 3’s original finding, was incomplete the first time anyone actually looked for shadow AI. Nothing in this book gives a reason to believe that a single look ever finds everything, and Calloway’s next inventory sweep is not guaranteed to find nothing new either.
None of the three organizations has reached a finished state, and none should expect to. A governance program that considered any of these three resolved would be exhibiting exactly the theater Chapter 17 warned against, mistaking the absence of a currently visible problem for the absence of one.

title: 18. Governing Under Uncertainty
text:
Summary
Compliance calendars fail because a regulatory date is a changeable estimate, not a plan. Over-investing against a date treated as fixed, and under-investing against a date treated as already moved, come from the same underlying mistake. The EU’s 2026 deferral and Colorado’s repeal-and-reenactment sequence show the pattern the legal record actually documents, while what any specific organization did in response is inference, not observed finding. Horizon scanning turns the underlying risk into a manageable operating discipline with a named owner and defined actors. That discipline includes sources selected for where change actually appears first, a cadence set by risk and source volatility rather than one fixed interval, and a triage step scoring authority, applicability, probability, lead time, and reversibility into more than a simple watch-or-act split. It also includes translation of what clears triage into a tracked, dated change request carried through implementation, validation, and closure. Regulation-agnostic design keeps a stable, regulation-neutral fact record separate from each regulation’s own independently evaluated mapping card. A regulation change touches only that regulation’s card, and no regulation’s own legal conclusion, such as a “high risk” label, is treated as another regulation’s input.
Beneath any specific regulation’s vocabulary, a set of reusable governance capabilities recurs, though not as identical legal duties. They are knowing what you have, assessing before deploying, testing for disparate effect, documenting, overseeing, monitoring, and responding, each required, permitted, narrowed, or omitted differently by any given regulation. A program built on this capability set is positioned to keep that infrastructure useful when a regulation’s name, threshold, or entire enforcement architecture changes. The field asks its practitioners for technical literacy without technical expertise, and legal literacy without legal training, kept separate from authoritative legal interpretation and backed by a qualified legal owner. It also asks for judgment to distinguish real risk from theater, and for the standing to say no as a delegated authority granted in advance rather than a personal trait. More than one axis of where the discipline is heading remains unsettled. This book’s own argument is that governance earns its return primarily by preventing the wrong system from being built in the first place, a rationale worth stating plainly without dressing it as a demonstrated business case the evidence does not yet support.

title: 18. Governing Under Uncertainty
text:
Review questions
COMPREHENSION

Explain the shared root cause behind over-investing against a regulatory date treated as immovable and under-investing against a date treated as already settled before it is law.
Explain why this chapter sets horizon-scanning cadence from source volatility and risk, not a single fixed interval, and describe two triage states, beyond simply watching or acting, that a proposal or a signed law might legitimately be assigned to.

APPLIED

A system’s fact record shows an employment use case with a given autonomy, scale, and affected population. Explain why this chapter says that record should not itself store a conclusion such as “high risk,” and what changes and what does not change in the system’s governance record when a regulation governing that use case is repealed and replaced with a different framework.
Using the reusable governance capabilities this chapter names, identify which chapter of this book each capability was originally established in, and explain why a specific regulation might require, permit, narrow, or omit any one of them rather than imposing an identical duty.

SPOT THE RISK

A governance program treats a proposed but not yet enacted regulatory delay as though compliance work against the original date can stop immediately. Identify what this chapter would say is at risk in that decision and what a properly run horizon-scanning triage step would have done differently.

COMPARE AND DECIDE

Compare classifying a system separately under each applicable regulation against classifying it once and maintaining a mapping to each regulation’s obligations, for an organization operating across multiple jurisdictions whose laws change independently of each other, and state which approach this book favors and why.

RUNNING CASE

MEDASSIST FAIRLEND TALENTSCREEN Using the case in focus, explain why this chapter declines to describe any of the three organizations’ governance programs as finished, and what risk that description itself would create if a governance program actually believed it.


Every chapter in this book has argued, in its own subject, for the same underlying discipline. Know what a system is before deciding what to do about it. Assess before deploying. Design controls proportionate to what is actually at stake. And keep the evidence that lets the organization demonstrate, rather than merely believe, that it did. The specific laws this book has cited will have moved again by the time it is read. That discipline is what was meant to survive the move.

title: Appendix A: Technique Reference
text:
The chapters apply several general information-gathering and analysis techniques without teaching them from first principles. This appendix is a pointer to what each technique is, when a chapter uses it, and where to look for a fuller treatment, not a substitute for learning any of them properly. Ordinary versions of most techniques assume a cooperative subject, and governance work frequently does not have one. Two techniques get real, worked treatment in their chapters instead of a pointer here for exactly that reason: consulting stakeholders who cannot be reached (Chapter 14, section 14.2) and questioning a vendor who has reason not to answer (Chapter 16, section 16.3). Look there, not here, for those two.
Affinity grouping. Sorting a large number of individually generated ideas, findings, or complaints into a smaller number of natural categories by inspecting them for similarity, not by imposing a category scheme in advance that the raw material might not actually fit. Use it after a brainstorming session or an open-ended survey has produced more individual items than a group can usefully discuss one at a time. See Chapter 3’s shadow AI discovery, where individually reported tools have to be grouped before they can be classified. For further reading, see any general text on qualitative data analysis.
Benchmarking. Comparing a system, a metric, or a process against a defined reference point, either an industry norm, a prior version of the same system, or a stated target, to establish whether a result is good, typical, or concerning. Use it when a number needs context to be interpretable on its own. See Chapter 7’s testing thresholds and Chapter 9’s drift baselines. For further reading, see any general text on quality measurement or statistical process control.
Brainstorming. Structured group generation of options or possibilities before evaluating any of them, deliberately separating idea generation from idea judgment so early criticism does not suppress options a group would otherwise have surfaced. Use it when a risk list, a use case list, or a set of candidate controls needs to be wide before it needs to be right. See Chapter 3’s inventory discovery and Chapter 14’s risk identification. For further reading, see any general text on group facilitation or creative problem solving.
Checklist review. Verifying a deliverable or a decision against a predefined, fixed list of required elements, catching omissions a less structured review would miss. It suits anything with a stable, enumerable set of requirements, such as a documentation package or a release gate. See Chapter 8’s deployment readiness review and Appendix C’s templates generally. For further reading, see any general text on quality assurance methods.
Decision matrix. A table scoring a small number of candidate options against a fixed set of weighted criteria, producing a total score per option that makes the basis for a comparison explicit instead of leaving it implicit in a group’s unstated intuitions. A weighted total is only as sound as the assumptions behind it. It assumes the scales across criteria are comparable and that a high score on one criterion can offset a low score on another. That assumption does not hold for a legal, safety, or rights requirement, which a low overall score should never be allowed to outweigh. Use it whenever more than two options are genuinely under consideration, the criteria that matter can be named in advance, and normalized scales are used. Run a sensitivity check to confirm the ranking survives reasonable changes in the weights. Apply any non-negotiable constraint as a gate before scoring, not by folding it into the score itself. See Chapter 6’s model selection factors and Chapter 13’s operating model comparison. For further reading, see any general text on multi-criteria decision analysis.
Document analysis. Extracting information from existing written material, policies, contracts, model cards, prior incident reports, rather than generating new information through interviews or observation. Use it before a live consultation whenever the timeline allows, since a question already answered in an existing document should not consume a stakeholder’s time, but do not let it delay input that is urgent on its own terms. An affected person’s immediate concern, an incident still unfolding, or a decision on a short deadline should not wait on a document review that could run in parallel instead. See Chapter 15’s evidence discipline and Chapter 16’s model card interrogation. For further reading, see any general text on qualitative research methods.
Facilitated workshop. A structured group session, run by a neutral facilitator, that brings multiple stakeholders together to reach a shared output, a classification scheme, a risk register, a target operating model, in one coordinated session instead of through separate interviews later reconciled by hand. Use it when the output requires agreement across roles, not aggregation of separate opinions. See Chapter 13’s operating model design and Chapter 17’s requirements gathering. For further reading, see any general text on group facilitation technique.
Five whys. A root cause technique that asks “why” repeatedly against a stated problem, each answer prompting the next why, until the questioning reaches a cause the organization can actually act on rather than a symptom one level removed from it. A single chain of whys tends to find one cause, but an incident, especially one involving people, process, and a system together, more often has several interacting contributory factors. Framing the technique as a search for the one root cause can end the inquiry too early. Or it can land on an individual’s action as the answer, when the actual conditions that made that action likely deserve equal attention. Use it when an incident’s immediate cause is obvious but its underlying cause is not. Treat multiple branches as a normal outcome, not a failure of the technique, and direct the questioning at conditions and system design instead of at assigning blame to a person. See Chapter 10’s incident investigation. For further reading, see any general text on root cause analysis, including fishbone or cause-and-effect diagramming as a related technique.
Focus group. A moderated group discussion with a small number of participants selected for a shared characteristic relevant to the question, used to surface reactions, concerns, or usability problems that individual interviews might not reveal through group dynamics alone. Use it when the goal is understanding a shared experience, not gathering independent facts. See Chapter 8’s pilot feedback and Chapter 17’s rollout evaluation. For further reading, see any general text on qualitative research methods.
Gap analysis. Comparing a current state against a defined target state and naming the specific, itemized distance between them, rather than describing either state in isolation. It fits whenever a target has been defined and the question becomes what stands between here and there. See Chapter 17’s current-to-target sequencing. For further reading, see any general text on organizational change management.
Interview, structured and semi-structured. A one-on-one or small-group conversation using a prepared set of questions, asked consistently across participants in a structured interview or adapted in response to what a participant says in a semi-structured one. Use a structured interview when comparability across participants matters most; use a semi-structured one when depth on an individual participant’s specific situation matters more than strict comparability. See Chapter 3’s inventory interviews, Chapter 14’s stakeholder consultation, and Chapter 17’s requirements gathering. For further reading, see any general text on interview technique in applied research.
Observation. Watching how people actually perform a task, in its ordinary setting, instead of asking them to describe it afterward, on the reasoning that a description of a workflow and the workflow itself frequently diverge without anyone intending to mislead. Use it whenever a workaround or an informal practice is suspected but has not been reported. See Chapter 17’s requirements gathering from what people do when a process becomes inconvenient. For further reading, see any general text on contextual inquiry or ethnographic method.
Peer review. Having a person with comparable expertise, but no direct authorship stake in the work, examine a decision, a document, or a finding before it is finalized. The reasoning is that a second qualified reader catches errors the original author’s own familiarity with the material makes hard to see. Reach for it when a finding will be relied on downstream, a classification decision, a risk score, an audit result, and a single unreviewed judgment carries more consequence than the added time a second reader costs. See Chapter 17’s discussion of a second reviewer disagreeing with the first as an outcome metric for whether classification is accurate. For further reading, see any general text on quality assurance in professional practice.
Prioritization scale. A method for ranking a list of items, risks, requirements, findings, into a small number of tiers by relative importance, forcing an explicit comparison instead of leaving every item marked equally important. A ranking assumes the items compared are the kind of thing capacity can trade off against each other. That is not true of a legal, safety, or rights duty, which the organization has no discretion to deprioritize regardless of where it lands on the list. Exclude those items from the ranking exercise, and treat them as required, not just highly ranked. Use it whenever the remaining, genuinely discretionary list is longer than an organization’s capacity to act on all of it at once, which is nearly always. See Chapter 14’s forced risk-ranking tiebreak and Chapter 15’s requirement priority field. For further reading, see any general text on requirements prioritization technique.
Process mapping. Diagramming the sequence of steps a workflow actually follows, including decision points and handoffs between roles, to make a process visible and discussable instead of implicit in individual habit. A map limited to steps and handoffs omits the evidence, controls, exceptions, and ownership a governance process also needs; add those elements before treating the map as complete. Use it before redesigning any workflow, so the redesign changes a documented reality rather than an assumed one. See Chapter 17’s control and workflow design. For further reading, see any general text on business process modeling.
RACI matrix. A table assigning, for each significant activity, exactly who is Responsible for doing the work, who is Accountable for the outcome, who must be Consulted before a decision, and who merely needs to be Informed after one. It resolves the ambiguity that produces both duplicated effort and dropped responsibility. “Exactly one accountable person per activity” is the matrix’s own operating convention rather than a universal organizational rule. It needs reconciling with a governing body’s oversight accountability, an executive’s ultimate accountability, and a control or assurance function’s independent accountability for checking the work, none of which a single RACI row is built to represent on its own. Use it whenever more than one role could plausibly own a task and the organization has not yet said which one does, alongside whatever governance and assurance accountability already sits above the activity level. See Chapter 13’s incident-response responsibility assignment. For further reading, see any general text on project or program governance.
Risk matrix. A grid plotting likelihood against severity, used to compare and prioritize risks on two dimensions simultaneously instead of collapsing them into a single combined score that hides which factor is driving a risk’s position. The ordinal categories a matrix typically uses, low, medium, high, compress a wide range of actual likelihood and severity into a small number of bins. This can rank two meaningfully different risks identically, or place a low-probability, catastrophic risk in the same cell as a frequent, minor one. Calibrate what each category actually means before using it, and treat a cell placement as a starting point for judgment rather than a finished conclusion. Set an explicit non-compensable threshold, too, such as any risk to life or an irreversible rights harm, that a matrix position alone cannot downgrade. Use it whenever a risk list needs comparison, not only enumeration, alongside a stated uncertainty about where a given risk actually falls. See Chapter 14’s risk scoring. For further reading, see Cox, “What’s Wrong with Risk Matrices?”, Risk Analysis 28(2), 2008, on the technique’s known ranking and categorization limits.
Sampling. Examining a subset of a population, selected either randomly or purposively, when examining the full population is impractical. Random selection on its own does not guarantee a representative or statistically defensible estimate. It requires a clearly defined sampling frame that actually covers the population of interest, a known or estimated probability of inclusion for each unit, and a stated plan for handling nonresponse or missing cases. Where the frame or response pattern is uneven, it also requires weighting to correct for it, together with a reported margin of uncertainty rather than a single point estimate presented as exact. Use random sampling, built this way, when the goal is a defensible estimate across the whole population; use purposive sampling when the goal is understanding specific, known cases of concern, and do not present a purposive sample’s findings as population-representative. See Chapter 9’s sampling-with-adjudication approach to delayed ground truth. For further reading, see any general text on sampling methodology in applied statistics.
Stakeholder mapping. Identifying every person or role with a genuine stake in a decision or a system, and characterizing each by their level of influence over the outcome and their level of interest in it. This lets engagement effort be allocated deliberately, not defaulted to whoever is easiest to reach. Influence and interest alone systematically underweight a person or group who is significantly affected by a system’s outputs but holds little organizational power over it. A mapping that stops there tends to concentrate engagement effort on internal stakeholders who are easy to reach, rather than on the people the system actually affects. Add the population’s expected impact, any heightened vulnerability, relevant rights, and the practical barriers a given group faces to participating at all. Use those added dimensions to correct engagement effort toward low-power, high-impact groups, instead of away from them. Use it at the start of any consultation effort, before deciding who to interview, survey, or convene. See Chapter 14’s stakeholder consultation and Chapter 17’s requirements gathering from developers, business owners, and reviewers. For further reading, see any general text on stakeholder analysis method.
Survey and questionnaire. A structured set of questions distributed to a larger group than an interview practically reaches, trading the depth of an individual conversation for coverage across a wider population. It fits when a finding needs to be established across a population instead of illustrated through individual cases. See Chapter 17’s training completion and rollout feedback collection. For further reading, see any general text on survey design.
SWOT analysis. A structured inventory of an initiative’s internal Strengths and Weaknesses alongside external Opportunities and Threats, used to surface a rounded picture before a decision rather than only the factors that first come to mind. Use it sparingly, only where a genuinely rounded picture, not a risk list alone, is what the decision requires. See Chapter 13’s operating model selection. For further reading, see any general text on strategic planning method.
Timeline reconstruction. Assembling a dated, sequential record of what happened, decision by decision and event by event, from logs, messages, and documents produced at the time rather than from participants’ later recollection of the order events occurred in. Use it for any incident investigation or post-mortem where the sequence of decisions matters as much as the decisions themselves. See Chapter 10’s incident documentation requirement that decisions be captured with timestamps as the response unfolds. For further reading, see any general text on incident investigation method.
Traceability matrix. A table linking each requirement to the specific evidence that demonstrates it was met, making a status claim checkable against a named artifact rather than asserted on memory. Use it wherever a later reviewer, internal or regulatory, will ask an organization to demonstrate rather than simply state that a requirement was satisfied. See Chapter 15, section 15.2, for this book’s full treatment. For further reading, see any general text on requirements management.
Voting and ranking techniques. Methods, including simple ranked voting and weighted-point allocation across a fixed budget, for converting a group’s individual preferences into a single prioritized list without one person’s opinion silently dominating the outcome. As with a prioritization scale, exclude a legal, safety, or rights requirement from the vote entirely rather than letting a group’s preference ranking decide whether the organization does something it has no discretion not to do. Use it, for the genuinely discretionary remainder of a list, after brainstorming has produced more candidate items than the group can act on and a shared ranking is needed to choose among them. See Chapter 13’s operating model decision process. For further reading, see any general text on group decision-making method.

title: Appendix B: Regulatory Quick Reference
text:
The EU AI Act: tiers and obligations
This appendix is a snapshot, not a living document. Every entry below was checked against the primary source named against it, current as of 12 September 2026. Regulatory dates move, as Chapter 18 spent an entire chapter demonstrating. A reader consulting this appendix more than a few months after publication should treat every date here as a starting point for a horizon scan rather than as a current fact, per the discipline Chapter 18, section 18.2 describes. Where a date or status could not be confirmed against a primary source, this appendix says so instead of printing an unverified figure.
The Act regulates by risk tier and allocates duties by role, established fully in Chapter 2. It sets out four tiers, presented below in descending order of obligation.
Unacceptable risk (Article 5). Prohibited outright are social scoring of natural persons, certain forms of biometric categorization and untargeted facial recognition database scraping, emotion inference in workplaces and schools, and exploitation of vulnerabilities. The 2026 Digital Omnibus added two more to the list, AI systems generating non-consensual sexually explicit deepfakes of identifiable people and AI-generated child sexual abuse material. The social-scoring prohibition reaches any deployer, public or private, not public authorities alone.
High risk (Article 6, Annexes I and III). The Act’s most detailed obligation set applies here, requiring a risk management system, data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, transparency to deployers, human oversight, and accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity. These obligations fall primarily on providers, with a narrower set on deployers. Annex III lists standalone high-risk use cases directly, including employment, creditworthiness, and law enforcement contexts this book’s running cases inhabit. Annex I covers high-risk AI embedded in products already regulated under EU product safety law.
Limited risk (Article 50). Article 50 attaches transparency duties to specific systems and actors, not to a residual bucket covering everything outside the other tiers. Providers and deployers must disclose that a person is interacting with an AI system, label synthetic content, and disclose deepfakes and AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest.
Minimal risk. Everything else, unregulated by the Act’s risk tiers, though general-purpose AI model obligations under Chapter V apply regardless of the risk tier of any downstream system built on such a model.

The deferral exists because the harmonized standards that would let a provider demonstrate compliance cheaply were not ready. As of this appendix’s check date, no CEN-CENELEC standard developed for AI Act purposes has been cited in the Official Journal, so the presumption of conformity Article 40 offers is not yet available to any provider on any standard. One standard, covering the quality management system obligation, cleared CEN-CENELEC’s own internal approval in mid-2026, which is a necessary step toward Official Journal citation but is not the citation itself. Do not treat a standard’s internal publication by a standards body as equivalent to its legal effect under the Act; only Official Journal citation confers the presumption.

title: Appendix B: Regulatory Quick Reference
section: EU AI Act conformity assessment routes
text:
EU AI Act conformity assessment routes
A high-risk system reaches the market through one of two routes. Internal control lets a provider self-assess conformity against the Act’s requirements and issue its own declaration, available for most Annex III use cases where a harmonized standard has been applied or where the provider can otherwise demonstrate the requirements are met. Third-party conformity assessment, through a notified body, is required for biometric identification systems and for products already subject to third-party assessment under other EU product law, such as medical devices. A provider using internal control still bears full legal responsibility for the system’s conformity; the absence of third-party review changes who checks the work, not what work must be done.

title: Appendix B: Regulatory Quick Reference
text:
United States: federal landscape
No single, complete federal AI statute has been enacted as of this appendix’s check date. Federal AI policy operates through executive action and agency guidance, not legislation. Executive Order 14365 set federal AI policy direction. Litigation testing its interaction with state law, including a challenge to Colorado’s now-superseded statute, produced a stipulated stay of enforcement rather than any ruling on the merits. No US court has ruled on the merits of a challenge to a state AI law as of the check date. A proposed decade-long moratorium on state AI enforcement was removed from a 2025 reconciliation bill by a 99 to 1 Senate vote. That is the clearest evidence available that federal preemption of state AI law is contested on grounds other than party. A discussion draft addressing preemption of state authority over AI model development specifically, without a bill number as of the check date, was released in mid-2026 by members of the House. Whether it has since been introduced as a numbered bill should be checked directly, not assumed either way.
NIST, an agency and not a legislature, has published the closest thing to federal technical guidance. See below.

Beyond the instruments tabled above, a distinct category of conversational AI and companion chatbot statutes emerged across roughly fourteen states during 2026, addressing AI interaction disclosure, self-harm response protocols, and safeguards for minor users. This appendix has not independently confirmed each state’s specific bill number and status. An organization operating a conversational AI product should treat this category as an active horizon-scanning priority, and verify the current instrument in each state where it operates instead of relying on the count above. Sector and public-sector laws also exist in a growing but still scattered set of states, addressing health insurance utilization review automation and public-sector AI use and procurement specifically. These generally sit at a lighter obligation level than the frontier-model and employment statutes tabled above, and are likewise better confirmed against a current state-by-state search than assumed from this snapshot.

title: Appendix B: Regulatory Quick Reference
text:
NIST AI Risk Management Framework
The AI RMF (NIST AI 100-1, published January 2023) organizes risk management into four functions, each with named categories. Govern cultivates an organizational culture and structure for AI risk management through policies and processes, accountability structures, workforce diversity in AI risk roles, organizational commitment to trustworthy AI characteristics, mechanisms for external stakeholder feedback, and policies addressing third-party and supply chain risk. Map establishes the context needed to frame risk correctly by understanding the deployment context, categorizing the AI system, documenting its capabilities and intended benefits and costs, mapping risks and benefits across system components, and mapping impacts to individuals, groups, and society. Measure applies quantitative and qualitative methods to analyze and track risk by identifying appropriate methods and metrics, evaluating the system for trustworthy characteristics including validity, safety, and fairness, tracking identified risks over time, and gathering feedback on how well the measurement approach itself is working. Manage allocates resources to the risks the first three functions surfaced by prioritizing and acting on risk, applying strategies to maximize benefit and minimize harm, managing third-party risk specifically, and documenting and monitoring risk treatments over time.
A companion Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1, published July 2024) maps these same four functions to risks specific to generative systems, including confabulation, harmful content generation, data privacy leakage through model outputs, and intellectual property concerns among others. Both documents remained the current, unrevised versions as of this appendix’s check date. NIST has stated the framework is under revision as part of a federal AI policy initiative, so a reader should check for a newer version before treating either document’s exact category list as final.

title: Appendix B: Regulatory Quick Reference
text:
ISO/IEC 42001: clause structure
ISO/IEC 42001:2023, the AI management system standard, follows the common high-level structure shared across ISO management system standards, making it straightforward to integrate into an organization already certified to a standard such as ISO 27001 or ISO 9001. Its numbered clauses proceed, in order, through Scope, Normative references, Terms and definitions, Context of the organization, Leadership, Planning, Support, Operation, Performance evaluation, and Improvement. An Annex lists specific AI management controls and objectives, covering policies related to AI, internal organizational roles, resources dedicated to AI systems, impact assessment, and the AI system life cycle. It also covers data governance for AI systems, information provided to interested parties, use of AI systems, and third-party and customer relationships.
The European Commission and its Joint Research Centre have stated that ISO/IEC 42001, while a useful foundation for an AI management system, is not aligned in objective with the specific quality management system the EU AI Act requires. ISO/IEC 42001 requires an AI system impact assessment covering individuals, groups, and societies, but its certification is not designed to satisfy the Act’s system-specific technical documentation and quality management provisions. An organization certified to 42001 has not thereby satisfied the Act’s quality management obligation, though the certification’s processes substantially overlap with what the Act separately requires.

title: Appendix B: Regulatory Quick Reference
section: Other standards worth knowing by name
text:
Other standards worth knowing by name
ISO/IEC 42005:2025 addresses AI system impact assessment specifically, the closest existing standard to Chapter 14’s subject. ISO/IEC 42006:2025 addresses requirements for bodies providing audit and certification of AI management systems. ISO/IEC 23894:2023 addresses AI risk management generally, a companion to 42001 rather than a competitor to it. ISO/IEC 38507:2022 addresses the governance implications of AI use for organizational governing bodies specifically, bearing on this book’s Chapter 13. Several further standards on human oversight, AI system logging, and quality models for AI systems were in late-stage development as of the check date and had not yet published; treat any reference to them elsewhere as forthcoming, not available.

title: Appendix B: Regulatory Quick Reference
text:
Sector-specific requirements
Healthcare. In the United States, whether a clinical decision support or diagnostic tool resembling this book’s MEDASSIST case needs premarket clearance or approval depends on a specific determination, not a general presumption. FDA guidance excludes certain clinical decision support functions from the statutory device definition outright, treats some other functions under enforcement discretion, and regulates the remainder as devices proportionate to risk. The same product can therefore contain both device and non-device functions. The determination has to be made function by function, against the device definition, the statutory exclusions, and current FDA guidance (checked 2026-09-13, per FDA’s Clinical Decision Support Software FAQs). Where a function is regulated as a device, ongoing obligations to report adverse events and material changes to its cleared function apply. The FDA has also issued guidance specifically addressing predetermined change control plans for AI-enabled devices whose performance is expected to update after initial clearance, directly relevant to Chapter 6’s model versioning and Chapter 9’s drift monitoring. Separately, HIPAA’s privacy and security requirements apply only where the organization is a covered entity or a business associate handling protected health information, not to health data generally or to every organization that touches it. An organization needs to determine its own HIPAA status independently of any FDA determination, since neither regulation’s applicability establishes the other’s. A product can be subject to one, both, or neither, depending on what it does and who operates it.
Financial services. In the United States, a credit decisioning system such as this book’s FAIRLEND case operates under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and its implementing Regulation B. This requires a specific and accurate statement of reasons when an application for credit is denied, the adverse action explanation this book’s Chapter 8 and Chapter 15 both address directly. Banking regulators, principally the Federal Reserve and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, have issued supervisory guidance on model risk management. This guidance predates the AI-specific frameworks this appendix otherwise covers. It is frequently the source of the model risk management function that Chapter 13 describes as a potential structural competitor to a newer AI governance function. That guidance’s scope should not be assumed to reach every AI model automatically. Interagency guidance updated in 2026 (Federal Reserve SR 26-2, effective 17 April 2026, superseding SR 11-7 and SR 21-8) applies its principles to traditional and non-generative, non-agentic AI models while expressly excluding generative and agentic AI models from that specific framework’s definition (checked 2026-09-13). An institution within SR 26-2’s scope needs to determine first whether a given system meets the guidance’s model definition before assuming existing model-risk infrastructure already covers it. A generative or agentic system excluded from that definition still needs governance, just not automatically through the model-risk-management channel. State insurance regulators separately govern algorithmic underwriting and pricing tools through unfair discrimination statutes that apply independently of any AI-specific statute a state might also enact, a survival this appendix’s Colorado entry notes directly.
Employment. Beyond the state and local statutes already listed above, the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has issued guidance applying existing anti-discrimination law, including disparate impact theory under Title VII, to algorithmic hiring tools without requiring new legislation to do so. This means an employment AI system such as this book’s TALENTSCREEN case carries discrimination-law exposure even in a jurisdiction with no AI-specific statute in effect. An organization operating in this sector should treat the absence of an AI-specific state law as silence on the new label, not an absence of applicable law.

Using this appendix
Nothing above substitutes for reading the primary source directly before relying on any specific obligation, threshold, or date in a real compliance decision. This appendix exists to orient a reader quickly across a landscape this book has already argued, in Chapter 18, cannot be captured permanently in any single document, including this one.
This appendix deliberately omits a dated comparison of specific model capabilities across providers. Such a comparison would be obsolete within a small number of months of this book’s printing, considerably faster than the regulatory dates above move. No comparison this appendix could print would remain a fair or current snapshot for long enough to be worth the space. A reader who needs current capability comparisons should consult a provider’s own published evaluation results, dated at the time of consultation, rather than any fixed table a printed book could offer.

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
1. AI Use Case Documentation
These nine templates are offered under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International (CC BY-NC 4.0) for readers to copy, adapt, and use directly in their own organizations. Reuse under that license has to satisfy its actual conditions, not a looser summary of them. The license requires attribution and a notice of changes made. Its NonCommercial term is defined by whether the use is primarily intended for or directed toward commercial advantage or monetary compensation, a broader test than resale alone. This paragraph is a summary for convenience, not a substitute for the license text itself, which a reader relying on these templates commercially or without attribution should read directly. Within those conditions, fill in the fields, cut what your organization does not need, add what it does, and use the result as a working document instead of treating this appendix as an illustration to reference from a distance. Each field below is cross-referenced to the chapter section that establishes it, so a filled-in template can be traced back to the specific requirement it satisfies.
Each template below is scoped to hold one record for one system, model, agent, or event; an organization with many systems keeps many filled instances of the same template instead of trying to make a single instance cover a portfolio. Fields marked as cross-references exist so the nine templates link into one connected set of records, rather than nine disconnected documents. That is what lets a later reviewer trace a specific system’s history across inventory, assessment, and incident records without reconstructing the connections from memory. Because a specific chapter’s model can itself be revised in a later edition, each template also carries the same minimal record-control header. That header records a template ID and version, the book edition and chapter section it was built from, and the date it was last checked against that section’s current text. That lets a later reviewer tell which version of a chapter’s model a specific filled instance was built against. Every filled instance should also carry its own status, author, reviewer, approver, effective date, and change history in addition to its substantive fields, following Chapter 15’s evidence-record discipline generally, not restating it individually in each template below.
Complete before any development or procurement work begins, per Chapter 4’s argument that governance starting after a system exists is inspection rather than governance.

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists

Use case name and one-sentence description
Business owner, naming a specific person and role, not a department alone, with the effective date this person took the role so the record stays traceable when the person changes

Why an AI approach specifically, as distinct from a rules-based or manual alternative
Expected benefit, and what happens if this use case is not pursued at all

2. System Inventory Record
One record per system, maintained per Chapter 3, section 3.3, as a living artifact with an owner and a review date, not a one-time exercise. A system discovered through the shadow AI discovery process in Chapter 3, section 3.4, uses this same record; note the discovery method in the last field rather than treating a discovered system as a different kind of record.

System name and internal identifier
Business owner and technical owner (may differ)
Business unit and physical or organizational location of use
System class: predictive, generative, or agentic
Deployment status: in development, piloting, in production, retired
Model or models used (cross-reference to Model Inventory Record entries)
Data sources and categories of personal data processed, if any
Risk classification and the date it was assigned (cross-reference to Impact Assessment)
Applicable regulatory mappings (Chapter 3, section 3.7; Chapter 18, section 18.3)
Date of last review and scheduled next review date
Record owner, last update date, and, if applicable, discovery method if this system was not originally self-reported

3. Model Inventory Record
One record per model, distinct from the System Inventory Record above because one model can serve several systems and one system can call several models, per Chapter 3’s system-versus-model distinction.

Model name and version identifier
Developer or source (internal build, fine-tune of a named base model, or purchased)
Path: build, fine-tune, adapter, or licensed third-party (Chapter 16, section 16.6)
Training data summary, or “not visible to this organization” where the path is buy (Chapter 5)

Known limitations and failure modes as currently understood
Systems this model serves (cross-reference to System Inventory Record entries)
Date last validated and validation method used
Reassessment triggers that would require re-validation (Chapter 14, section 14.5)

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists

4. Model Card
For a model an organization builds or fine-tunes itself. For a purchased model, use this same structure to record what the vendor has and has not disclosed, per Chapter 15’s adversarial reading approach, marking undisclosed fields explicitly instead of leaving them blank.

Model name, version, and date
Intended use and explicitly out-of-scope uses
Training data description, covering sources, time period, and known composition, or the vendor’s disclosed description quoted directly if this organization cannot see the underlying data
Performance metrics, the population and methodology they were measured against, and the date measured
Fairness testing summary, covering metrics used, populations compared, and findings (Chapter 7)
Known limitations and documented failure modes
Safety and refusal behavior notes, where applicable (Chapter 11)
Retraining or update history and how a user of this card is notified of changes
Contact point for questions this card does not answer

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
5. Impact Assessment
Follow Chapter 14’s five-component structure as it stands in this book’s current text. That structure is itself the subject of ongoing refinement across this book’s own chapters, so record which edition and check date this template instance was built against rather than assuming the structure is fixed for all time. Complete before deployment, and again whenever a reassessment trigger fires. Where a stakeholder who would normally be consulted cannot be reached, record which of Chapter 14’s consultation substitutes was used instead and what it cannot recover compared to direct consultation.

System description, covering what it does, who it affects, and at what scale
Risk identification, listing each identified risk, its likelihood and severity (Chapter 14, section 14.3), and its source
Mitigation, naming the specific control addressing each risk and whether it reduces the risk’s occurrence or only detects it after the fact (Chapter 14, section 14.4)
Residual risk, stating what remains after mitigation explicitly instead of leaving it implied by silence
Documented decision, naming the accountable approver, the date, and the specific reasoning accepting the residual risk or requiring further mitigation before proceeding
Reassessment trigger conditions and next scheduled review date

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
6. Vendor Assessment
Structured across Chapter 16’s four assessment dimensions, built against this book’s current chapter text and, like template 5, worth re-checking against a later edition rather than assumed fixed. Log every question the vendor declined to answer in the final field; a declined question is itself evidence.

Provider dimension, covering company stability, support commitments, and track record
System dimension, covering what the model actually does, its documented limitations, and disaggregated performance data if obtainable
Documentation dimension, covering model card completeness, per template 4 above, and what is missing
Compliance dimension, covering applicable certifications, audit rights offered, and regulatory mappings the vendor supports
Contract provisions confirmed present, covering information rights, audit rights, change notification, incident cooperation, liability allocation, and exit terms (Chapter 16, section 16.5)
Questions the vendor declined to answer, and whether each decline is disqualifying (Chapter 16, section 16.3)
Overall recommendation and named approver

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
7. Agent Registration and Permission Scope
One record per agentic system or agent role, per Chapter 12’s argument that an agent’s authority must be recorded before it acts, not reconstructed afterward.

Agent name and the system it belongs to (cross-reference to System Inventory Record)
Issuing authority, naming who approved this agent’s credential and on what basis
Subject and audience, naming the actor the credential is issued to and the resource or party it is valid against
Scope of authority, naming the specific actions, resources, and purposes this agent is permitted to invoke without further human approval, and what is explicitly out of scope
Tools and systems this agent can access, and the permissions granted to each
Credential form and validity, describing how the scope is technically enforced (a scoped, time-bound credential per Chapter 15, section 15.5), its validity window, and its current revocation state
Policy decision point, naming what evaluates a given action against this scope at runtime and what happens on a policy denial
Escalation conditions, naming what triggers a required human-in-the-loop step and the approval and result recorded when one fires
Logging requirements, naming what is captured at each action, including the scope in force at the time of the action, a correlation ID linking related actions, and a tamper-evident integrity mark on the record (Chapter 15, section 15.5)
Monitoring, naming what ongoing check confirms this agent is not exceeding its recorded scope in practice and how an exception surfaces
Delegation chain, if this agent can invoke or supervise other agents, including each hop’s own scope and whether it can be narrower or wider than the delegating agent’s own
Review cadence and the date of last permission-scope review
Deregistration or scope-revocation process, who is authorized to invoke it, and what recovery or rollback applies to actions already taken under a credential later found to have been wrongly scoped

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
8. Incident Response
Structured per Chapter 10’s response sequence. Open a record at the moment an incident is identified, not after it is resolved.

Incident identifier, date and time first identified, and detection source (monitoring, user report, audit, vendor notice, or other)
Accountable owner for the response, named at the point the record is opened
Severity classification and the criteria that produced it
Systems and populations affected
Evidence preservation, naming what was captured before any remediation altered the system’s state and where it is retained
Containment actions taken, and the date and time each was taken
Assessment, stating what is currently known about scope and cause, updated as it changes, including root cause and any contributory factors distinct from it (Chapter 10’s investigation approach)
Communication log, naming who was notified, when, and with what content, kept current through resolution instead of written once at closure
Regulatory reporting determination, stating whether a notification obligation applies, under which specific regulation, in what role (for example, an EU AI Act operator’s serious-incident duty under Article 73), the applicable deadline measured from awareness, and the status of any required interim and final reports
Affected-party remedy, naming what correction, compensation, or other remedy was offered or provided, to whom, and when
Rollback or recovery, naming what was reverted or restored and confirming that the reversion actually took effect
Documentation of decisions made during the response, each with a timestamp and the name of who made it
Corrective action and its verification, naming the specific process or control change the incident produced and how its effectiveness was confirmed instead of only implemented
Closure criteria met, post-incident review date, and the lesson fed back into the relevant control, template, or training material
For a system with delayed or absent ground truth (Chapter 9), the method used to establish how many cases were actually affected, since a prevented or undetected outcome leaves no confirmed case to count directly

title: Appendix C: Templates and Checklists
text:
9. Governance Readiness
Per Chapter 17. Use this to conduct a current-state assessment, not to describe an aspirational future state.

Inventory assurance, meaning the percentage of known systems with a current inventory record, plus a separate estimate of unknown-system exposure from the date and method of the last discovery sweep (Chapter 3’s shadow AI discovery). A percentage of known systems alone cannot measure what the inventory has not yet found
Classification coverage, giving the percentage of inventoried systems with a current risk classification
Process versus practice, stating for each governance process that exists on paper whether it is actually used, for what proportion of applicable systems, and evidence supporting that answer (Chapter 17, section 17.2)
Requirements gathered, giving the date of last consultation with developers, business owners, and reviewers on where the process obstructs their work
Control proportionality, stating whether review depth is tied to risk tier or applied uniformly regardless of it
Cost model, stating whether each control’s cost has been estimated at production volume rather than pilot volume
Training completion, giving the percentage of each role trained and the date of last training update
Outcome metrics, covering issues found before deployment versus after, classification accuracy on independent review, and bypass rate by system and by team
Named owner of this readiness assessment and date completed
